segments.say: Oskar steps off the train into a fine rain and walks the ten minutes home. Before his key is in the lock he can hear claws on the floorboards. Pepper greets him as though he has been away for a year, turns two circles, performs a long stretch with her front paws pushed far out ahead, and then yawns right up at him.

He catches it, naturally. But the more interesting question runs the other way. When a person yawns, can a dog catch it? Dogs have lived alongside humans for thousands of years, and they're famously attentive to our faces, our voices and our moods. If any animal were going to pick up our yawns, a dog would be a reasonable candidate.

In 2008, Ramiro Joly-Mascheroni, Atsushi Senju and Alex Shepherd tested twenty-nine dogs. In one session, a person unfamiliar to the dog yawned while facing it, again and again, for five minutes. In a comparison session, the same sort of person made mouth movements, opening and closing, without the features of a real yawn.

show.who: Ramiro Joly-Mascheroni, Atsushi Senju and Alex Shepherd
show.what: A stranger yawns at a dog

segments.say: The result was dramatic. Twenty-one of the twenty-nine dogs, about seventy-two percent, yawned while the person was yawning. None yawned during the comparison session. That's a higher proportion than is often seen in adult humans watching videos, and it was widely reported as the first evidence that a yawn could pass from our species to another.

It's the kind of result that asks to be repeated, and repetitions have been mixed. Some later studies found much weaker effects, and others had difficulty finding contagious yawning in dogs at all. Researchers have discussed whether stress might explain part of it, since dogs sometimes yawn when they're uneasy, and a stranger yawning directly at them is a slightly odd experience.

Elainie Madsen and Tomas Persson in Sweden asked a developmental question, much like the one asked about children. They tested thirty-five young dogs, from about four to fourteen months old. A person, either their familiar owner or an unfamiliar researcher, yawned at them in one phase and made a plain gaping movement in another.

Among the older young dogs, from about seven months, yawns drew more yawning than plain gapes did. Among the younger ones, from four to six months, the difference wasn't reliable, partly because they also responded to the gapes. And whether the person was their owner or a stranger didn't make a clear difference in this study.

show.title: What the puppy study found
items: Older puppies yawned more to yawns than to gapes
Younger ones showed no clear difference
Owner or stranger made no reliable difference

segments.say: That suggests the tuned response, to yawns in particular, may sharpen as a dog grows up, a little like the change we saw in children around the age of four. The authors were careful to say that the youngest dogs might respond to open mouths in a more general way at first. Development shapes this behaviour, in at least two species.

A well-worn dog bed beside a radiator. Pepper has already returned to hers and is watching Oskar take off his wet coat, chin on her paws. Every so often their eyes meet. This quiet checking on one another, dozens of times an evening, is the setting in which a cross-species yawn would have to travel.

show.cap: A dog bed beside a warm radiator

segments.say: You're welcome to yawn near your own dog and see what happens. It's harmless if you do it gently and don't loom. Just remember what a single kitchen trial can't tell you. A dog may yawn because it's late, because it's mildly unsure why you're staring, or because dogs yawn quite often anyway. One yawn proves very little.

Cat owners often ask about their own companions. Cats certainly yawn, generously and with great style. Whether they catch our yawns is much less studied, and I don't know of firm evidence either way. If your cat yawns back at you, enjoy the moment. If it looks at you with complete indifference, that is also very much in character.

So for dogs: one well-known study found most of its twenty-nine dogs yawning when a person did. Later research hasn't always agreed. A study of young dogs suggested a response specific to yawns develops with age. And any yawn from any dog can have several causes, which keeps the researchers honest.

show.title: Dogs in brief
items: One 2008 study: 21 of 29 yawned to a human
Puppies seemed to grow into it
Stress and plain timing can confuse the picture

segments.say: Taken together, the animals add something to our evening. The spontaneous yawn is very widespread and probably very old. The contagious yawn seems rarer, shows up in some highly social creatures, tends to develop with growing up, and in several observations favours companions. That's consistent with a social side to yawning, while leaving its exact job open.

Oskar fills the kettle and leans against the counter while it begins to murmur. It's late, and the kitchen is warm and dim. Pepper has padded in after him and settled across his feet. For the first time since early morning, nothing is being asked of him. He yawns, slowly and without any hurry at all.

This one feels different from the yawn on the train. Nobody started it. It rose by itself, from the end of a long day, as the body began its turn toward sleep. It's one of those yawns from the diaries, the ones that gather in the hours before bed. A doorway yawn, if you like, marking the way from one state into the next.

Waiting for the water, he runs over what he's picked up. The oxygen story didn't hold up when tested. Yawns bunch around waking, sleeping and dull stretches. Cooling and arousal are serious ideas. Contagious yawns grow in during childhood, differ widely between adults, and may travel more easily between those who are close.

And what nobody knows yet is just as clear: exactly what a yawn does for the body, and exactly why another person's can set it going. Oskar finds he doesn't mind. There's something pleasant about carrying a mystery that is this small, this harmless and this close at hand. He can look into it again every single day.

show.sub: An open question at the end of the day

segments.say: The kettle clicks off. From here on, there's nowhere further to travel. We'll gather the evening's ideas gently, think about what a yawn might ask of us, and then let the house, and your own room, grow quiet. There's no need to follow closely any more. Just keep us company for as long as you like.
